clue.text: Friends of king in square dance

indicators.note: the king letter is placed inside the jumbled letters
to dance is to move about, so the letters of the word square are jumbled

parts.note: K is the chess and card abbreviation for king

explanation.surface: Some royal companions join in a square dance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'dance' turns SQUARE into QUAERS, and 'in' puts K inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: The Religious Society of Friends is the formal name of the Christian group whose members are popularly called by this name.

clue.text: Mercy shown in hanging procedure?

definitions.meaning: showing mercy to a beaten enemy, sparing their life, is the old military sense here
the old traitor's sentence of being hanged, drawn and then cut into four pieces

explanation.surface: Clemency granted during an execution.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means clemency shown to a foe, and also the cutting into four parts that ended a traitor's hanging and drawing.

clue.text: Attack like sailor out of turn

parts.note: as means like, in comparisons

indicators.note: the sailor's word sits outside the turn, so it wraps it

parts.note: an old salt is an experienced sailor
a U-turn, so U stands for a turn

explanation.surface: A sailor lashes out when he is not on watch.
explanation.walkthrough: 'out of' puts the sailor round U, as in U-turn. 'out of turn' looks like the idiom for speaking or acting improperly, which suits the attack.
explanation.definitionFit: An assault is a violent attack on a person or position.

clue.text: Disciples said to be 2 of it?

definitions.text: Disciples said to be 2 of it?

parts.words: Disciples said to be 2 of it?
parts.note: Jesus told his followers they were the salt of this, and salt is the sailor in the clue to 2 down

explanation.surface: Asks what Christ's followers were called the salt of.
explanation.walkthrough: In the Sermon on the Mount Jesus calls the disciples the salt of this world; the 2 points to SALT in the 2 down wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase 'salt of the earth', from Matthew's gospel, is what Christ called his disciples.

clue.text: Partner going off when there's no going on

parts.note: food going off is turning stale
a mate is a partner

explanation.surface: A spouse leaves when the relationship can go no further.
explanation.walkthrough: STALE (going off) and MATE (partner), written in answer order. In chess this is the position where no legal move remains.
explanation.definitionFit: Stalemate is a deadlock, a situation in which no further progress or move can be made.

clue.text: Force called for an outer garment

indicators.note: something called out is spoken, so the clue goes by the sound of the word

parts.note: the Force is a common name for the police

explanation.surface: The police are summoned on account of some coat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'called' says the word for Force, POLICE, is said aloud; spoken with a soft first syllable it sounds like the coat's name.
explanation.definitionFit: A pelisse is a long cloak or fur-trimmed jacket worn over other clothing, as by hussars.

clue.text: Instruments to put "p" into pastries

indicators.note: the letter is put into the pastries word, inside it

parts.note: pies are baked pastries

explanation.surface: A baker's odd instruction to add a letter to some tarts.
explanation.walkthrough: 'into' puts P inside PIES.
explanation.definitionFit: Pipes are wind instruments, such as bagpipes or panpipes.

clue.text: The French strip for one to give them a wash

definitions.text: one to give them a wash

parts.note: la is a French word for the
to strip is to undress

explanation.surface: French people undress so somebody can wash them.
explanation.walkthrough: LA (French for 'the') + UNDRESS (strip). 'them' in the definition means clothes.
explanation.definitionFit: A laundress is a woman whose job is washing and ironing clothes and linen.

clue.text: Majestic as "Unter den Linden"?

parts.note: German for under the, and sub means under
linden is another name for the lime tree

explanation.surface: Praises Berlin's grand boulevard as stately.
explanation.walkthrough: Unter den Linden is Berlin's grand avenue, literally 'under the limes': SUB (under) + LIME (linden).
explanation.definitionFit: Sublime means of outstanding grandeur or beauty, awe-inspiring and majestic.

clue.text: Eastern resolution may be of importance

indicators.note: a resolution breaks something into parts and re-forms it, so the letters of eastern are re-sorted

explanation.surface: A determination from the East may be weighty.
explanation.walkthrough: 'resolution' rearranges EASTERN. 'resolution' reads as determination, which the answer also suggests.
explanation.definitionFit: Earnest can mean serious or weighty, of a matter deserving grave attention.

clue.text: American occupying halls in Europe

indicators.note: to occupy a place is to sit inside it, so one piece sits within the other

parts.note: atria are entrance halls, the plural of atrium
US is short for United States, so American

explanation.surface: A US citizen takes up residence in some halls on the continent.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is loose, 'in Europe' standing for a country found there; the clue would read as a sentence with Austria's name in place of those words.
explanation.definitionFit: Austria is a landlocked country in central Europe, so it is one place in that continent.

clue.text: Worker in softwood with 5 down

parts.note: the soft part: p, for piano, is the musical direction meaning soft
the wood part: lumber is timber, wood sawn for building

explanation.surface: A tradesman who handles pine planks along with some pipes.
explanation.walkthrough: Split 'softwood' into soft (P, piano) and wood (LUMBER). 'with 5 down' adds that the worker uses pipes, the answer to 5 down.
explanation.definitionFit: A plumber is a tradesperson who fits and repairs water pipes, so a kind of worker.

clue.text: What wielding those guns is intended to convey?

definitions.text: What wielding those guns is intended to convey?

indicators.note: wielding means handling and swinging about, so the letters of those guns are moved around

explanation.surface: Asks what message a gunman brandishing weapons is trying to send.
explanation.walkthrough: 'wielding' rearranges THOSE GUNS; the whole clue also defines it, since brandishing guns is meant to look hard.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone brandishing firearms wants to project hardness and resilience, the quality of being tough.

clue.text: Force redhead into disreputable resort

indicators.note: one piece goes into the other, so it sits inside it

parts.note: a dive is a seedy bar or club
the head of the word red is its first letter, R

explanation.surface: A ginger-haired person pushed into a seedy bar.
explanation.walkthrough: 'into' puts R, the head of 'red', inside DIVE, a seedy bar.
explanation.definitionFit: To drive is to force or compel, as in driving someone to despair.

clue.text: Church teaching put about in services

parts.note: RI is religious instruction, as taught in British schools

indicators.note: about signals turning round, so the word for put is read backwards

parts.note: to set something is to put it down

explanation.surface: Doctrine of the church spread around during worship.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' reverses the word for put. RI, religious instruction, is a British school subject, so church teaching.
explanation.definitionFit: Rites are religious ceremonies, the formal services of a church.

clue.text: Car helps one to get round

indicators.note: to get here means to be made into, so the letters are reshaped

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: A vehicle aids someone in going around.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to get' rearranges CAR HELPS plus I, the Roman one.
explanation.definitionFit: Spherical means shaped like a ball, perfectly round.

clue.text: Surprise at men working over notorious prison

indicators.note: the jumbled letters lie over and around the prison, holding it
working means in operation or in action, so the letters of at men are set to work in a new order

parts.note: the Maze was a high-security prison in Northern Ireland, notorious during the Troubles

explanation.surface: Astonishment as men toil above an infamous jail.
explanation.walkthrough: 'working' rearranges the two short words into AMENT, which 'over' wraps around the prison. The Maze, near Belfast, held paramilitary prisoners during the Troubles.
explanation.definitionFit: Amazement is the feeling of great surprise or wonder.

clue.text: Dead taken from northeast town to the cemetery

indicators.note: the abbreviation is removed from the town's name

parts.note: Darlington is a town in County Durham, north-east England

explanation.surface: A body carried from a northern town to the graveyard.
explanation.walkthrough: 'taken from' removes D (dead) from DARLINGTON. Arlington National Cemetery, Virginia, is the US military burial ground.
explanation.definitionFit: Arlington National Cemetery is the famous American military graveyard near Washington.

clue.text: Swell, see?

parts.note: the S of Swell is read as the compass abbreviation for south
the rest of Swell is simply the letters well

explanation.surface: A two-word quip: a posh fellow asking whether you get it.
explanation.walkthrough: Read 'Swell' as S + WELL and expand S to SOUTH. A see is a bishop's diocese; the Nottinghamshire town has a minster and its own diocese.
explanation.definitionFit: Southwell is the seat of a Church of England diocese, and a bishop's seat or diocese is called a see.

clue.text: Seasons for sex aids?

definitions.meaning: the warmest seasons of the year, plural
sex is Latin for six; people who add up figures help reach such totals

explanation.surface: Asks whether the warm months help with romance.
explanation.walkthrough: Read the second part as sum-mers, people who do sums; 'sex' is Latin for six, a total they might reach.
explanation.definitionFit: The word names the hottest seasons, and also people who calculate sums, read as sum-mers.

clue.text: Up is up with long short letter

indicators.note: in a down clue, up means the word is read from bottom to top, so backwards
short means cut off, so the final letter of long is removed

explanation.surface: A riddling sentence about something lengthy being brief.
explanation.walkthrough: The second 'up' turns IS into SI, as this is a down entry; 'short' cuts G from LONG, leaving LON.
explanation.definitionFit: Upsilon is the twentieth letter of the Greek alphabet.

clue.text: One sticks to one's post

parts.note: reads like a loyal guard who never leaves duty, but describes the gummed item that adheres to a letter in the mail

explanation.surface: Praise for a sentry who never deserts duty.
explanation.definitionFit: A postage stamp is stuck onto an item of mail, so it literally clings to the post.

clue.text: Like 22 may be, but no more than usual

annotationWithheld.why: Like 22 may be, but no more than usual (7) AVERAGE: 'no more than usual' defines it, but no parse of 'Like 22 may be' (22 is MISER) gives the letters; perhaps an unexplained pun on avarice
annotationWithheld.clue: Like 22 may be, but no more than usual

clue.text: Media constrain the establishment to wobble

indicators.note: to constrain is to hold in, so the press letters enclose the other piece

parts.note: the press is the news media
CE is the Church of England, the established church

explanation.surface: Journalists hold back the powers that be.
explanation.walkthrough: 'constrain' holds one piece inside the other. The Church of England is the established church, so the establishment; press is a loose stand-in for all the media.
explanation.definitionFit: To precess is to wobble the axis of a spinning body, as a gyroscope or the Earth does.

clue.text: No time for Mister Scrooge

indicators.note: no time means the abbreviation for time is removed from the word

explanation.surface: A Christmas tale's Mr Scrooge has no spare moment.
explanation.walkthrough: 'No time' takes T (time) out of MISTER.
explanation.definitionFit: Ebenezer Scrooge, the Dickens character, is the archetypal skinflint, so his name stands for a hoarder of money.

clue.text: Can't one see how to make a start with a foreign language?

indicators.text: how to make a start with
indicators.note: the answer makes its start with the opening words of the clue, which hold it in their letters

parts.note: a learner's despairing question, but its opening three words run together spell out a Chinese tongue spoken in Guangzhou and Hong Kong

explanation.surface: A frustrated learner wonders how to begin studying a new language.
explanation.walkthrough: 'how to make a start with' says the answer begins the clue: it runs through CANT ONE SEE, ignoring the apostrophe and the final E.
explanation.definitionFit: This Chinese language of Guangzhou and Hong Kong is foreign to English speakers.

clue.text: Rebel took time as a trainee

parts.note: Jack Cade led a rebellion in Kent in 1450

explanation.surface: An insurgent took time out to train.
explanation.walkthrough: Jack Cade led the 1450 English revolt; add T (time).
explanation.definitionFit: A cadet is a young trainee in the armed forces or police.

clue.text: Primate suffering from fruit shortage

indicators.note: a shortage is a lack, so the fruit word is short of its final letter

parts.note: an orange is a fruit

explanation.surface: An ape is ill because there is not enough food.
explanation.walkthrough: 'shortage' cuts E from ORANGE. Orang is short for orang-utan.
explanation.definitionFit: Orang is a shortened name for the orang-utan, a great ape of Borneo and Sumatra.

clue.text: Cleaned out and tangled together

indicators.note: out here means put out of order, so the letters of cleaned are rearranged

explanation.surface: Something scrubbed out and knotted up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'out' rearranges CLEANED.
explanation.definitionFit: To enlace is to entwine or interlace, so enlaced things are wound together.

clue.text: Hardwood — pine, say — pleasant when toasted

indicators.note: say tells you to speak the words, using their sound rather than spelling

parts.note: teak is a tropical hardwood and to pine is to ache, giving teak ache

explanation.surface: Discusses timber, then suggests something nice once heated.
explanation.walkthrough: 'say' tells you to speak TEAK ACHE aloud: it sounds like the toasted bun. Pine looks like a tree, but here it is the verb to long for.
explanation.definitionFit: A teacake is a light sweet bun, usually with dried fruit, eaten split, toasted and buttered.

clue.text: One-time underwear

parts.note: single means one, alone

explanation.surface: Undergarments from a bygone era.
explanation.walkthrough: 'One-time' looks like 'former', but splits into SINGLE (one) and T (time).
explanation.definitionFit: A singlet is a sleeveless vest worn under a shirt, a piece of underclothing.

clue.text: Weapon recoils and bags chicken, perhaps

indicators.note: a gun recoils by springing backwards, so the word for weapon is read backwards

parts.note: a gun is a weapon
to bag something is to get or catch it

explanation.surface: A gun kicks back as the hunter catches poultry.
explanation.walkthrough: 'recoils' turns GUN into NUG, followed by GETS (bags).
explanation.definitionFit: Chicken nuggets are the classic example of these small bite-sized pieces of food.
